content: Rosuvastatin is recognized as one of the most potent statins currently available and is widely prescribed for lipid-lowering purposes. Understanding the dose-dependent effects of rosuvastatin on blood lipid levels is crucial for optimizing its clinical use. The primary objective of this review was to quantify the effects of different doses of rosuvastatin on serum total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides in individuals with or without cardiovascular disease. Secondary objectives included assessing the variability in the lipid-lowering effects of rosuvastatin at various doses and evaluating the frequency of withdrawals due to adverse effects (WDAEs) in randomized placebo-controlled trials. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science Core Collection, and BIOSIS Citation Index, covering studies published up to late 2014. No language restrictions were applied. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials and uncontrolled before-and-after trials that evaluated the dose-response relationship of fixed doses of rosuvastatin over a period of three to 12 weeks. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies and extracted relevant data. Information on WDAEs was specifically collected from placebo-controlled trials. The review included 108 trials, comprising 18 placebo-controlled studies and 90 before-and-after trials, involving a total of 19,596 participants. Rosuvastatin doses ranging from 10 to 40 mg/day were associated with reductions in LDL cholesterol of 46% to 55%, based on pooled data analyzed using the generic inverse variance method. The quality of evidence supporting these effects was rated as high. Analysis of log dose-response data across doses from 1 to 80 mg demonstrated a strong linear relationship between rosuvastatin dose and reductions in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and non-HDL cholesterol. When compared to atorvastatin, rosuvastatin exhibited approximately three times the potency in lowering LDL cholesterol. Rosuvastatin did not show a dose-dependent effect on HDL cholesterol levels. However, overall, it increased HDL cholesterol by an average of 7%. The trials included in this review were noted to have a high risk of bias, particularly in relation to WDAEs, but this bias was unlikely to have influenced the lipid-lowering measurements. In 10 out of 18 short-term placebo-controlled trials, the incidence of WDAEs was not significantly different between rosuvastatin and placebo groups (risk ratio 0.84; 95% confidence interval 0.48 to 1.47). In conclusion, the lipid-lowering effects of rosuvastatin on total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and non-HDL cholesterol were found to be linearly dependent on dose, with a clear log dose-response relationship over the commonly prescribed dose range. Rosuvastatin demonstrated approximately threefold greater potency compared to atorvastatin in reducing LDL cholesterol. However, the review did not provide a reliable estimate of the incidence of adverse effects associated with rosuvastatin due to the short duration of the included trials and the lack of adverse effect reporting in 44% of the placebo-controlled studies.
